common_name: Flying Colors Coral Diascia (Vivid Coral Twinspur)

planting.note: Set out rooted cuttings or nursery starts after the soil has warmed slightly, since Flying Colors Coral establishes best once nights stay reliably above freezing but before summer heat arrives.

directions: Flying Colors Coral is a Proven Winners twinspur selected for its saturated, deep coral blooms and unusually tight, upright bloom spikes that hold their color well even under strong summer light. Grow it in fast-draining, evenly moist soil with excellent air movement, since diascia resents soggy roots and stagnant humidity around its foliage. Water in the morning rather than late in the day to keep the compact mound of small leaves dry overnight, and shear plants back lightly after the first major flush to renew branching and extend bloom into fall.
sources: Cornell University Bluegrass Lane Flower Trials

common_name: Flying Colors Apricot Diascia (Shimmering Apricot Twinspur)

planting.note: Transplant after hardening off once frost danger has passed; Flying Colors Apricot branches quickly from a young start and fills in containers or border edges within a few weeks.

directions: Flying Colors Apricot produces warm, shimmering apricot flowers on a well-branched, mounding plant that Cornell trial evaluations have noted for holding its color under high summer light and heat better than many older diascia strains. Plant in well-drained soil enriched with organic matter and keep moisture consistent, since the shallow root system dries out quickly in fast-draining containers. Deadhead spent spikes and shear lightly after the first bloom flush to keep the plant compact and encourage repeat flowering through the cooler shoulder seasons.
sources: Cornell University Bluegrass Lane Flower Trials

common_name: Sun Chimes Burgundy Diascia (Large-Flowered Burgundy Twinspur)

planting.note: Plant out young starts once nighttime lows are reliably above the mid-30s F; Sun Chimes Burgundy performs best where spring and fall stay cool and mild.

directions: Sun Chimes Burgundy is bred for noticeably larger individual flowers than most twinspur cultivars, carried in dusky burgundy-red racemes over a low, spreading mound of foliage. Give it humus-rich, well-drained soil and regular water, since the trailing stems and broad flowers wilt quickly if the root zone is allowed to dry out completely. Because bloom quality declines once temperatures climb into the heat of summer, plan for it as a spring and autumn container or edging plant, refreshing with a light trim and feeding to encourage a strong second flush as weather cools.

common_name: Whisper Pumpkin Diascia (Compact Deep Orange Twinspur)

planting.note: Set out transplants after hardening off; the compact Whisper series fills small containers and basket edges quickly without needing to be pinched hard.

directions: Whisper Pumpkin brings a deep orange flower color that stands apart from the pinks and reds typical of most twinspur breeding, held on the same low, well-branched habit that makes the Whisper series popular for hanging baskets and mixed containers. Grow in well-drained, evenly moist soil and avoid overhead watering late in the day to reduce foliar disease in humid climates. Shear lightly after each bloom cycle to maintain the tight, mounding form and to push out fresh flower spikes once summer heat eases.

planting.note: Transplant rooted cuttings or nursery starts after frost danger passes; Bluebird tolerates a wider temperature range than many nemesia and can go out slightly earlier than heat-sensitive strains.

directions: Bluebird is a long-popular Nemesia fruticans selection valued for its deep purple-blue, yellow-eyed flowers and a sweet, clove-like scent that intensifies in full sun. Its semi-trailing, well-branched stems suit hanging baskets and window boxes as well as border edges, and it tends to hold up to temperature swings better than many newer nemesia hybrids. Keep soil consistently moist and shear the plant back by about a third after each bloom flush to maintain dense growth and encourage continued flowering from spring through fall.

common_name: Berries and Cream Nemesia (Fragrant Bicolor Purple-and-White Nemesia)

planting.note: Plant out after hardening off once the danger of hard frost has passed; Berries and Cream blooms fastest and most heavily in cool, mild weather.

directions: Berries and Cream carries a bicolor flower unusual among nemesia, pairing purple-blue upper petals with a white lower lip and a small yellow eye, and it is one of the more strongly scented cultivars in cultivation. Grow it in fertile, slightly acidic, well-drained soil and keep watering consistent, as this compact, bushy plant has a fine root system that suffers quickly if it dries out. Deadhead regularly through the growing season to keep the plant flowering from spring into fall, and expect a lull in the hottest weeks of summer followed by renewed bloom as temperatures moderate.

common_name: Aromatica Royal Blue Nemesia (Fragrant Dark Blue Nemesia)

planting.note: Transplant after hardening off once nights stay reliably above freezing; give plants a sheltered spot with good airflow to preserve the strong fragrance on still evenings.

directions: Aromatica Royal Blue is part of a fragrance-bred Ball FloraPlant series and stands out for larger, darker blue flowers than the standard Aromatica strain, backed by a noticeably sweet scent that carries well near patios and doorways. Plant in well-drained, moisture-retentive soil in full sun, and water at the base to keep the fine foliage dry and reduce the risk of fungal spotting in humid climates. Pinch young plants once to encourage branching, then shear lightly after the first bloom cycle to keep the habit tidy and extend flowering into the cooler weeks of fall.

common_name: Poetry Blue Nemesia (Fragrant Violet-Blue Bicolor Nemesia)

planting.note: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant out once nights stay above the mid-40s F; Poetry Blue is a compact seed-grown strain suited to cell-pack production.

directions: Poetry Blue is a seed-propagated nemesia strain bearing violet-blue flowers with a contrasting pale cream throat, forming a neat, mounding plant well suited to packs, small pots, and border edging. Sow indoors on the soil surface under light, since the fine seed needs light to germinate, and transplant once seedlings are well rooted and outdoor nights have warmed. Pinch young plants to encourage branching and deadhead through the season to keep the fragrant flowers coming, expecting a natural slowdown during the hottest stretch of summer.

common_name: Sunsatia Mango Nemesia (Fragrant Upright Orange Nemesia)

planting.note: Plant transplants after hardening off into well-drained, fertile soil; Sunsatia Mango's upright habit makes it better suited to patio pots and border fronts than hanging baskets.

directions: Sunsatia Mango carries warm, mango-orange flowers with a strong sweet fragrance on an upright, well-branched plant, distinguishing it from the more trailing colors in the Proven Winners Sunsatia series and making it a good fit for upright pots and mixed border plantings. Grow in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun and keep moisture consistent, since the fibrous root system does not tolerate extended drying between waterings. Deadhead and shear lightly to renew bloom through the cool months of spring and fall, expecting flowering to slow during the peak heat of summer before picking back up as temperatures drop.
